families.name: Two Pointers & Array Scanning
families.why: The cheapest way to turn an O(n^2) pair search into O(n). Almost every array problem starts by asking: can I move two indices instead of nesting two loops?

patterns.name: Opposite-End Two Pointers (sorted input)
patterns.trigger: Array is sorted or you are allowed to sort it, AND the objective is monotone as you move either end (pair sum, distance, area). Also: 'find a pair/triplet satisfying X'.
patterns.tmpl: lo=0, hi=n-1. Compare f(lo,hi) with target: too small -> lo++ ; too big -> hi--. Each element is visited once, so O(n) after the O(n log n) sort.
patterns.cx: O(n log n) sort + O(n) scan

patterns.name: Same-Direction Two Pointers (read/write in-place)
patterns.trigger: 'Modify the array in place', 'O(1) extra space', 'remove/reorder elements and return the new length', stable partition by a predicate.
patterns.tmpl: write=0; for read in range(n): if keep(a[read]): a[write]=a[read]; write+=1. Variants use 3 pointers (Dutch National Flag) when there are 3 buckets.

patterns.name: Fast & Slow Pointers in Value Space (Floyd)
patterns.trigger: Array where a[i] is itself a valid index (functional graph). 'Find the duplicate without modifying the array in O(1) space.' 'Each node has exactly one outgoing edge.'
patterns.tmpl: Treat i -> a[i] as a linked list. slow=a[slow], fast=a[a[fast]] until they meet; then reset one to the head and walk both one step at a time to find the cycle entry.

probs.t: Find the Winner of an Array Game
Maximum Employees to Be Invited to a Meeting

patterns.name: Cyclic Sort / Index-as-Hash
patterns.trigger: n elements with values confined to [1..n] or [0..n]. 'Find the missing / duplicated / mismatched number' with O(1) extra space.
patterns.tmpl: Either swap a[i] to position a[i]-1 until settled, or mark presence by negating a[abs(x)-1]. Then a single scan reveals which index is wrong.

probs.t: Find All Duplicates in an Array
Largest Positive Integer That Exists With Its Negative

patterns.name: Sort-Then-Pair / Greedy Matching
patterns.trigger: Two multisets to match up, or one set to pair internally, optimising a sum/count. Words like 'assign', 'match', 'team up', 'boats', 'pairs with difference <= k'.
patterns.tmpl: Sort both sides. Then either walk two pointers from the same end (greedy assignment) or from opposite ends (minimise max pair). Prove with an exchange argument.

patterns.name: Next Permutation / Lexicographic Construction
patterns.trigger: 'Next greater arrangement', 'k-th smallest string', 'smallest number greater than X with property'. Anything that needs the lexicographic successor.
patterns.tmpl: Scan from the right for the first i with a[i]<a[i+1]. Find the rightmost j>i with a[j]>a[i], swap, then reverse the suffix. The suffix is always non-increasing before the swap.

families.name: Prefix Sums, Difference Arrays & Line Sweep
families.why: When a question asks about many ranges, stop thinking about the ranges and start thinking about their boundaries. This family is the single highest-yield trick in contests.

patterns.name: Prefix Sum + HashMap (count subarrays with a property)
patterns.trigger: 'Number of subarrays whose sum equals / is divisible by / has parity k' AND the array can contain negatives or zeros (so sliding window is illegal).
patterns.tmpl: Keep running sum S. For each i, the count of valid j is freq[S - k] (or freq[S mod k]). Seed the map with {0:1}. The moment you see 'count subarrays' + 'negatives allowed', reach for this.

probs.t: Number of Sub-arrays With Odd Sum
Count Subarrays With Majority Element I

patterns.name: Prefix XOR
patterns.trigger: XOR over ranges, 'count subarrays with XOR = k', 'even count of each vowel/letter'. XOR is self-inverse so prefix works exactly like sums.
patterns.tmpl: pre[i] = a[0]^...^a[i]. XOR(l..r) = pre[r]^pre[l-1]. For parity-of-counts problems, compress the state into a bitmask and hash the first occurrence of each mask.

patterns.name: Difference Array (range update, offline query)
patterns.trigger: Many range updates followed by reads, or 'add val to every index in [l, r]' repeated q times. Constraints like n,q <= 1e5 make per-update O(r-l) too slow.
patterns.tmpl: diff[l]+=val; diff[r+1]-=val. One prefix-sum pass at the end reconstructs the array. Combine with binary search when the question is 'how many operations are needed'.

probs.t: Minimum Moves to Make Array Complementary
Maximum Frequency of an Element After Performing Operations II

patterns.name: 2D Prefix Sum
patterns.trigger: Submatrix sums, 'count submatrices with sum = target', 'largest square with sum <= threshold'. Grid dimensions up to a few hundred.
patterns.tmpl: P[i][j] = sum of the rectangle (0,0)-(i,j). Rectangle sum = P[r2][c2]-P[r1-1][c2]-P[r2][c1-1]+P[r1-1][c1-1]. For 'count = target', fix a row pair and fall back to pattern 2.1 on the columns.

patterns.name: Prefix + Suffix Precompute (split-point scan)
patterns.trigger: 'For every index, I need aggregate info about everything to its left AND right', 'split the array into two parts', 'product except self', 'without division'.
patterns.tmpl: Build left[] in a forward pass and right[] in a backward pass, then answer index i in O(1). If memory matters, keep the answer array as left[] and fold the suffix in during the reverse pass.
patterns.cx: O(n) time, O(1) extra if folded

patterns.name: Line Sweep / Event Counting
patterns.trigger: Intervals + 'maximum number overlapping at any moment', 'minimum rooms/servers/groups', or values that turn on at t1 and off at t2.
patterns.tmpl: Emit (start,+1) and (end,-1), sort by coordinate (ties: -1 before +1 if endpoints are exclusive), sweep and track a running counter and its maximum. When coordinates are huge, compress or use a hashmap keyed by coordinate.

families.name: Sliding Window
families.why: The window is not one pattern, it is six. Interviewers and contests distinguish them by the shape of the constraint, so this family is where most pattern-recognition errors happen.

patterns.name: Fixed-Size Window
patterns.trigger: The window length k is given in the statement. 'Every subarray of length k', 'k consecutive', 'k-size'.
patterns.tmpl: Add a[i]; once i >= k-1, record the answer and remove a[i-k+1]. One add and one remove per step keeps it O(n). Never rebuild the window.

Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K

Find X-Sum of All K-Long Subarrays I

patterns.name: Variable Window - Longest Valid (shrink while invalid)
patterns.trigger: 'Longest subarray/substring such that <constraint>' where the constraint is monotone: shrinking a valid window keeps it valid.
patterns.tmpl: for r: add a[r]; while invalid(): remove a[l]; l++ ; ans=max(ans, r-l+1). The invariant is that after the while loop the window is always valid.

probs.t: Longest Subarray of 1's After Deleting One Element

patterns.name: Variable Window - Shortest Valid (shrink while valid)
patterns.trigger: 'Minimum length subarray/substring such that <constraint>'. Note the flipped while-condition versus 3.2 - this is the single most common mix-up.
patterns.tmpl: for r: add a[r]; while valid(): ans=min(ans, r-l+1); remove a[l]; l++. You record the answer *inside* the while, not after it.

patterns.name: Exactly-K via atMost(K) - atMost(K-1)
patterns.trigger: 'Exactly k distinct', 'exactly k odd numbers', 'sum exactly equal to goal' on a non-negative array. A direct window cannot maintain 'exactly'.
patterns.tmpl: Write a helper atMost(k) as a standard 3.2 window returning the *count* of subarrays (each step adds r-l+1). Then answer = atMost(k) - atMost(k-1). Memorise the r-l+1 counting step.

probs.t: Count the Number of Good Subarrays

patterns.name: Window + Monotonic Deque (rolling min/max)
patterns.trigger: You need max or min *of the current window* in O(1), or a DP transition dp[i]=best(dp[j]) over a sliding range of j.
patterns.tmpl: Deque holds indices with decreasing values (for max). Pop from the back while the new value beats them, pop from the front when the index falls out of the window. Front is always the window max.
patterns.cx: O(n), each index pushed and popped once

patterns.name: Circular / Two-Ended Window
patterns.trigger: 'Circular array', 'take elements from either the front or the back', 'wrap around'. Both reduce to a contiguous window on a transformed array.
patterns.tmpl: For circular: duplicate the array or work mod n. For take-from-both-ends: taking k from the ends == leaving a contiguous window of n-k in the middle. Invert the problem, then run 3.2.

patterns.name: Window with Frequency Matching
patterns.trigger: Anagrams, permutations, 'contains all characters of t', 'every character appears exactly k times'. The validity check is a whole frequency vector.
patterns.tmpl: Maintain a 'matched' counter instead of comparing whole maps. Increment matched only when a character's count hits its exact requirement; the window is valid when matched == required distinct count.
patterns.cx: O(n * alphabet) worst case, O(n) typical

families.name: Binary Search
families.why: Half of all 'hard' contest problems are an easy problem wrapped in a binary search on the answer. Learning to spot monotonicity is worth more than learning any single algorithm.

patterns.name: Boundary Binary Search (lower / upper bound)
patterns.trigger: Sorted data + 'first index >= x', 'last occurrence', 'how many are less than x', 'for each query find the best prefix'.
patterns.tmpl: Standardise on ONE template: lo=0, hi=n (exclusive), while lo<hi: mid=(lo+hi)//2; if pred(mid): hi=mid else lo=mid+1. Return lo = first index where pred is true. Never write ad-hoc <= / < variants.

patterns.name: Binary Search on Rotated / Unknown-Shape Arrays
patterns.trigger: 'Sorted but rotated', 'mountain array', 'exactly one element appears once in a sorted array'. Local comparison still tells you which half to discard.
patterns.tmpl: At mid, determine which side is sorted (a[lo]<=a[mid]) and whether the target lies inside it; recurse into that half. For mountains, compare a[mid] with a[mid+1] to pick the slope.
patterns.cx: O(log n), O(n) worst for duplicates

patterns.trigger: THE tell: 'minimum possible largest ...', 'minimise the maximum', 'smallest capacity/speed/time such that it is feasible'. Value range is huge (1e9) but n is small (1e5).
patterns.tmpl: Define feasible(x) = 'can we do it if the cap is x'. feasible is monotone false...false,true...true. Binary search the smallest true. The feasibility check is usually a simple greedy O(n) scan.

patterns.trigger: 'Maximum possible smallest ...', 'largest minimum distance/candies/score'. Same machinery, feasibility flipped (true...true,false...false).
patterns.tmpl: feasible(x) = 'can we achieve at least x for everyone'. Binary search the largest true: while lo<hi: mid=(lo+hi+1)//2 (bias up) ; if feasible(mid): lo=mid else hi=mid-1.

patterns.trigger: 'k-th smallest' where materialising all candidates is impossible (pairs, products, multiples). n^2 candidates but the value range is searchable.
patterns.tmpl: Binary search on the VALUE v. countLessEqual(v) is computed with two pointers or per-row binary search. Find the smallest v with count >= k. The answer is guaranteed to be an actual element.

patterns.trigger: Offline queries against a sorted structure: 'for each query, the best value among items with weight <= q'. Sort once, prefix-max once, binary search per query.
patterns.tmpl: Sort items by the key you filter on. Build a running best/prefix array. Each query becomes an upper_bound plus an O(1) lookup. Sorting the queries too turns it into a single linear merge.

families.name: Stacks & Monotonic Structures
families.why: If a problem talks about 'the next element that is bigger/smaller' or about nesting, a stack is almost always the O(n) answer to an O(n^2) question.

patterns.name: Bracket / Expression Stack
patterns.trigger: Parentheses, nesting, matching, evaluating an expression, or anything with an opening and closing marker.
patterns.tmpl: Push openers, pop on closers and validate. For evaluation, push the accumulated result and sign when you meet '(' and restore on ')'. For 'minimum removals', count unmatched closers greedily and leftover openers at the end.

patterns.name: Monotonic Stack - Next/Previous Greater or Smaller
patterns.trigger: 'For each element, find the next element that is greater/smaller', 'how many days until warmer', 'span', 'the first taller building to the right'.
patterns.tmpl: Iterate once; while stack top violates the monotonic order, pop and resolve that popped index (the current element is its 'next greater'). Push the current index. Everything is pushed and popped once.

patterns.name: Monotonic Stack - Contribution Counting
patterns.trigger: 'Sum over ALL subarrays of min/max', 'count subarrays where a[i] is the maximum', 'total area of all rectangles'. Summing per subarray is O(n^2); summing per element is O(n).
patterns.tmpl: For each i find prevSmaller and nextSmaller. i is the minimum of exactly (i-prev)*(next-i) subarrays. Multiply by a[i] and add. Handle ties by making one side strict to avoid double counting.

probs.t: Maximum Score of a Good Subarray
Minimum Operations to Make Array Equal to Target

patterns.name: Monotonic Stack - Lexicographic Greedy Pop
patterns.trigger: 'Smallest/largest possible result after removing k characters', 'remove duplicate letters so the result is lexicographically smallest', 'build the best subsequence of length k'.
patterns.tmpl: Push characters; while the stack top is worse than the current char AND you can still afford to drop it (k>0, or the char appears again later), pop. Track a 'used' set when each char may appear once.

patterns.name: Stack Simulation - Collisions & Adjacent Cancellation
patterns.trigger: Elements interact only with their immediate neighbour and may annihilate: asteroids, adjacent duplicates, robots, path components, 'remove all occurrences of substring'.
patterns.tmpl: Push; before pushing, resolve conflicts against the top in a while loop; the current element may itself be destroyed (use a flag / else-clause on the while).

families.name: Heaps, Top-K & Scheduling
families.why: A heap is what you reach for when you need 'the current best' repeatedly while the set keeps changing. Recognising WHICH dimension to heap on is the real skill.

patterns.name: Top-K with a Heap (and the Quickselect alternative)
patterns.trigger: 'k largest / smallest / most frequent', 'k-th largest'. k is much smaller than n, or the data arrives as a stream.
patterns.tmpl: For k largest, keep a MIN-heap of size k (push, then pop when size>k). The heap root is the answer. Interviewers love the follow-up: Quickselect gives O(n) average for the offline case.
patterns.cx: O(n log k) heap, O(n) average Quickselect

patterns.trigger: 'Median of a stream', 'keep the top half and bottom half balanced', 'sum of the k smallest while elements keep arriving'.
patterns.tmpl: Max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper half; rebalance so sizes differ by at most one. Use lazy deletion (a 'removed' counter map) when elements must be revoked.

patterns.trigger: 'Merge k sorted lists/arrays', 'smallest range covering an element from each list', 'k pairs with the smallest sums'.
patterns.tmpl: Seed the heap with the first element of each list along with its (listIdx, elemIdx). Pop the min, push its successor. The heap size stays at k.

patterns.trigger: Tasks/meetings/customers with arrival times and durations; 'process in order of availability'; 'which room/chair/server is free'.
patterns.tmpl: Sort by arrival. Keep a min-heap of 'busy until' times and a heap/set of free resources. Advance the clock to the next arrival or the next release, whichever comes first. Two heaps, one loop.

families.name: Intervals
families.why: Interval problems all collapse into three questions: do they overlap, how many overlap, and which subset should I keep. Learn the three and you have covered the whole space.

patterns.name: Merge & Insert Intervals
patterns.trigger: 'Merge overlapping intervals', 'insert a new interval', 'remove covered intervals'. Output is a set of intervals, not a count.
patterns.tmpl: Sort by start. Walk the list keeping a current interval; if next.start <= cur.end, extend cur.end = max(cur.end, next.end), else flush cur and start a new one.

patterns.name: Interval Scheduling Greedy (max non-overlapping)
patterns.trigger: 'Maximum number of non-overlapping intervals', 'minimum removals to make them disjoint', 'minimum arrows/shots'. Output is a count.
patterns.tmpl: Sort by END time (not start). Greedily take an interval whenever its start is after the last taken end. Sorting by end is the exchange argument that makes it optimal - memorise the distinction from 7.1.

patterns.trigger: Online insertions with a rule like 'no triple booking'; 'how many events are active at time t'; a calendar that must reject conflicting bookings.
patterns.tmpl: Small n: keep a sorted list and check neighbours. Large/online: a hashmap of deltas (+1 at start, -1 at end) plus a running sum, or a dynamic/segment tree over compressed coordinates.

families.name: Hashing & Counting
families.why: Not glamorous, but roughly a third of all easy/medium problems are 'pick the right key for the hashmap'. The skill is choosing the canonical key.

patterns.name: Frequency Map & Pair Counting
patterns.trigger: 'Count pairs (i,j) such that f(a[i]) == g(a[j])'. Rearrange the condition until both sides involve only one index, then hash one side.
patterns.tmpl: Rewrite a[i]+rev(a[i]) == a[j]+rev(a[j]) style conditions so each side depends on a single element. Then iterate once, adding freq[key] to the answer BEFORE inserting the current element.

families.name: Linked List
families.why: Low algorithmic depth, high interview frequency, and unforgiving about pointer bugs. Drill these until the dummy-node and reversal skeletons are automatic.

patterns.name: Pointer Reversal
patterns.trigger: 'Reverse', 'reverse between positions m and n', 'reverse in groups of k', 'compare with the reversed half'.
patterns.tmpl: prev=None; while cur: nxt=cur.next; cur.next=prev; prev=cur; cur=nxt. For sub-range reversal, park a pointer at the node BEFORE the range and reconnect afterwards. Draw the three pointers before you type.

patterns.name: Dummy Head + Splice / Partition
patterns.trigger: Any operation where the head itself may change, or where you build several output chains: merge, partition, split into parts, remove nodes.
patterns.tmpl: Always allocate dummy=Node(0); dummy.next=head and return dummy.next. Build separate chains with their own tails and stitch them at the end. This removes every head-is-null special case.

probs.t: Delete Nodes From Linked List Present in Array

patterns.name: List + Auxiliary Structure
patterns.trigger: You need random access, prefix sums, or a stack over a list: deep copy with random pointers, remove zero-sum sublists, remove nodes with a greater node to the right.
patterns.tmpl: Either hash old-node to new-node, or run pattern 2.1 (prefix sum + map) over the list, or reverse-then-monotonic-stack. Recognise the underlying array pattern and apply it to nodes.

families.name: Trees
families.why: Trees are where recursion becomes intuition. Almost every tree problem is one of: aggregate from children, carry state down, or process level by level.

patterns.name: Postorder Aggregation (ask children, combine, return)
patterns.trigger: The answer involves subtrees: diameter, max path sum, 'is this subtree balanced/BST', coin distribution, count of nodes satisfying a subtree property.
patterns.tmpl: THE key move: the function RETURNS the value a parent can use, while the global answer is updated inside. These are usually different quantities (return the best downward path, but update the answer with left+right+node).

patterns.name: Root-to-Leaf Path DFS (carry state down)
patterns.trigger: 'All paths from root to leaf', 'sum of numbers formed by paths', 'path sum equals target', 'pseudo-palindromic paths'.
patterns.tmpl: dfs(node, stateSoFar). Append on entry, recurse, pop on exit (backtracking). For counting-based conditions, a bitmask carried down beats a list.

patterns.name: Level-Order BFS
patterns.trigger: 'Level by level', 'right side view', 'largest value in each row', 'zigzag', 'minimum depth', 'first node at the deepest level'.
patterns.tmpl: queue with a for-loop over len(queue) at the start of each level, so you always know the level boundary. That single snapshot of the size is what makes level logic clean.

patterns.name: Lowest Common Ancestor Family
patterns.trigger: 'Lowest common ancestor', 'distance between two nodes', 'directions from p to q', 'the k-th ancestor'.
patterns.tmpl: Plain LCA: return node if it is p or q; recurse both sides; if both return non-null, this node is the LCA. For repeated queries use binary lifting (pattern 13.6).
patterns.cx: O(n) per query, O(log n) with lifting

patterns.name: Build / Reconstruct a Tree
patterns.trigger: 'Construct the tree from preorder and inorder', 'from a traversal string with depth markers', 'from a list of parent-child descriptions'.
patterns.tmpl: Preorder gives the root, inorder splits left from right. Hash value->inorder index to make the split O(1), and pass index ranges rather than slicing arrays.

patterns.name: BST Properties (inorder is sorted)
patterns.trigger: The word 'binary search tree' plus anything about order, minimum difference, k-th smallest, mode, range sum, or validation.
patterns.tmpl: Inorder traversal of a BST is a sorted sequence. Keep a 'prev' pointer during inorder and compare - that solves validation, min-difference, and mode in one skeleton. Reverse inorder gives descending order.

patterns.name: Tree as Graph / Re-rooting
patterns.trigger: 'All nodes at distance k', 'infection spreading from a node', 'answer for every node treated as the root'. You need to move UPWARD, not just downward.
patterns.tmpl: Either build a parent map and BFS on the undirected graph, or do the two-pass re-rooting DP: one DFS to compute subtree answers, a second to push the outside-the-subtree contribution down.

patterns.trigger: 'Find duplicate subtrees', 'delete duplicate folders', 'are these two trees equivalent under flips'.
patterns.tmpl: Serialise each subtree postorder into a canonical string (or map strings to integer ids to keep comparisons O(1)) and count occurrences in a hashmap.
patterns.cx: O(n) with id-mapping, O(n^2) with raw strings

families.name: Graph Traversal
families.why: Most graph problems never name a graph. Learning to see the implicit graph - states, grids, words, dependencies - is the whole game.

patterns.name: Grid Flood Fill (DFS / BFS on a matrix)
patterns.trigger: A 2D grid with connected regions: islands, provinces, enclaves, sub-islands, regions cut by slashes.
patterns.tmpl: for each unvisited cell: start a DFS/BFS, mark everything reachable, count one component. Border-seeded traversal is the trick for 'closed' or 'surrounded' variants: flood from the border first, whatever is left is enclosed.

patterns.name: Multi-Source BFS
patterns.trigger: 'Everything spreads at the same time', 'distance to the NEAREST X for every cell', 'how many minutes until all oranges rot'. Multiple starting points.
patterns.tmpl: Push ALL sources into the queue at level 0 before you start popping. One BFS then gives every cell its distance to the nearest source. Do not run n separate BFS runs.

patterns.name: BFS on an Implicit / State Graph
patterns.trigger: 'Minimum number of moves/steps/transformations'. The nodes are states (a string, a board configuration, a tuple), not given vertices. Unweighted transitions.
patterns.tmpl: Define encode(state), define neighbours(state), then run a plain BFS with a visited set. Bidirectional BFS halves the work when both endpoints are known.

patterns.name: BFS with an Extra State Dimension
patterns.trigger: 'You may remove up to k obstacles', 'collect keys', 'each edge can be used twice', 'at most k stops'. Plain visited[] is wrong - you need visited[node][extra].
patterns.tmpl: State = (cell, remainingBudget) or (cell, keyBitmask). visited becomes a 2D/3D array. The moment a problem adds a budget or a collection requirement, expand the state.

patterns.name: 0-1 BFS (deque)
patterns.trigger: Edge weights are only 0 and 1 (or 'free move vs cost-1 move'): flipping a sign, removing one obstacle, changing direction.
patterns.tmpl: Use a deque: push weight-0 edges to the FRONT, weight-1 edges to the BACK. This keeps the deque monotone, so you get Dijkstra's result without the log factor.

patterns.name: Cycle Detection & Safe States
patterns.trigger: 'Is there a cycle', 'which nodes lead only to terminal nodes', 'the longest cycle', 'each node has exactly one outgoing edge'.
patterns.tmpl: Directed: DFS with three colours (white/grey/black); a grey neighbour means a cycle. Undirected: DFS with a parent check, or Union-Find. Functional graphs: iterative walk with a visit-timestamp array.

patterns.name: Bipartite / 2-Colouring
patterns.trigger: 'Split into two groups such that no two conflicting items share a group', 'is the graph bipartite', 'possible bipartition'.
patterns.tmpl: BFS/DFS colouring each neighbour with the opposite colour; a conflict means not bipartite. Must be run from every unvisited node (the graph can be disconnected).

probs.t: Divide Nodes Into the Maximum Number of Groups

patterns.name: Topological Sort (Kahn / DFS)
patterns.trigger: Dependencies, prerequisites, 'build order', 'is the ordering possible', 'the earliest finish time' on a DAG.
patterns.tmpl: Kahn: compute in-degrees, queue every 0-in-degree node, pop and decrement. If you process fewer than V nodes there is a cycle. DP along the topological order handles longest-path and counting questions.

probs.t: Find All Possible Recipes from Given Supplies

patterns.name: Eulerian Path / Circuit (Hierholzer)
patterns.trigger: 'Use every EDGE exactly once', 'reconstruct the itinerary', 'valid arrangement of pairs'. Note: every edge, not every node.
patterns.tmpl: Check degree conditions, then run Hierholzer: DFS greedily consuming edges, and append the node to the answer AFTER its edges are exhausted. Reverse the result at the end.

families.name: Shortest Paths
families.why: Four algorithms cover everything. The interview skill is picking the right one from the constraints in under ten seconds.

patterns.name: Dijkstra (non-negative weights)
patterns.trigger: Weighted edges, all non-negative, single source, 'minimum cost/time/effort to reach'. V up to 1e5.
patterns.tmpl: Min-heap of (dist, node). Pop, skip if dist > best[node], relax neighbours. The relaxation function is what varies: sum for cost, max for 'minimum effort', product for probability.

patterns.name: Dijkstra with State / Layered Graph
patterns.trigger: 'At most k stops', 'you may refuel/teleport twice', 'count the number of shortest paths', 'the second shortest path'.
patterns.tmpl: Node becomes (vertex, extraState). dist is 2D. For counting shortest paths, carry a ways[] array and add on equality, reset on strict improvement.

probs.t: Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination
Second Minimum Time to Reach Destination

patterns.name: Floyd-Warshall (all pairs)
patterns.trigger: V is small (<= ~400), you need distances between EVERY pair, or the problem asks 'for each city/node, count reachable nodes within a threshold'.
patterns.tmpl: Triple loop with k in the OUTER position: d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k]+d[k][j]). Getting k outermost is the single most common bug.

patterns.trigger: 'Minimise the maximum edge on a path', 'largest safety factor', 'the earliest day you can still cross'. A path exists only above/below some threshold.
patterns.tmpl: Binary search the threshold; the check is a plain BFS/DFS/DSU on the subgraph of allowed edges. Often you can skip the binary search with a max-heap Dijkstra where relaxation uses max() instead of sum.

families.name: Union-Find, MST & Graph Structure
families.why: DSU is the answer whenever the question is about connectivity rather than paths, and it is the backbone of every offline-query graph trick.

patterns.name: Union-Find Basics
patterns.trigger: 'How many connected components', 'are these two in the same group', 'redundant edge', merging equivalence classes. No path length is asked - only membership.
patterns.tmpl: parent[] with path compression in find(), plus union by size/rank. Memorise a 12-line class; you will paste it twenty times. Keep a components counter and decrement on each successful union.

patterns.name: DSU with Offline Sorted Queries (Kruskal-style)
patterns.trigger: Queries carry a threshold ('is there a path where every edge < limit', 'points reachable with value < q'). Answering each query independently is too slow.
patterns.tmpl: Sort edges by weight AND queries by threshold. Sweep the threshold upward, unioning every edge below it, then answer the query with a find(). Each edge is added exactly once across all queries.

patterns.name: Minimum Spanning Tree (Kruskal / Prim)
patterns.trigger: 'Connect all points/nodes at minimum total cost', 'the minimum cost to make the graph connected'. Complete graphs from coordinates are a strong hint.
patterns.tmpl: Kruskal: sort all edges, union greedily, stop after V-1 edges. Prim: heap-based, better on dense graphs. For critical/pseudo-critical edges, rerun Kruskal while forcing or forbidding one edge.

patterns.name: DSU on Grids & Swap-Group Reasoning
patterns.trigger: 'You may swap elements if they satisfy a relation' - the relation induces components, and within a component you can permute freely.
patterns.tmpl: Union indices that are swappable, then sort the values inside each component and write them back to that component's sorted positions. Also the standard trick for 'add one cell and get the biggest island'.

patterns.name: Bridges & Articulation Points (Tarjan)
patterns.trigger: 'Critical connection', 'removing this edge disconnects the network', 'find all cut vertices'.
patterns.tmpl: DFS with disc[] and low[]. Edge (u,v) is a bridge when low[v] > disc[u]. Keep a timer and skip the immediate parent edge.

patterns.name: Binary Lifting
patterns.trigger: Many queries of the form 'the 2^k-th ancestor', 'LCA of many pairs', 'jump k steps in a functional graph'.
patterns.tmpl: up[k][v] = up[k-1][up[k-1][v]]. Preprocess in O(n log n), answer each jump/LCA in O(log n) by decomposing k into bits.
patterns.cx: O(n log n) build, O(log n) query

families.name: Backtracking & Recursion
families.why: When n is tiny (<= 20) and the question says 'all', 'every', or 'count the ways with no formula', the intended solution is exhaustive search with pruning.

patterns.name: Subsets / Power Set
patterns.trigger: 'All subsets', 'every possible combination of items', n <= 20. Also any problem where you iterate over 2^n masks.
patterns.tmpl: Two equivalent skeletons: recursive take/skip at each index, or iterate mask from 0 to 2^n-1 and read the set bits. Sort first and skip duplicates with 'if i>start and a[i]==a[i-1]: continue'.

probs.t: Sum of All Subset XOR Totals
Count Number of Maximum Bitwise-OR Subsets
Maximum Number of Achievable Transfer Requests

patterns.name: Combinations (choose-k / combination sum)
patterns.trigger: 'All combinations of size k', 'all ways to reach target using the given numbers', order does not matter.
patterns.tmpl: backtrack(start, path): loop i from start to n, take a[i], recurse with i (reuse allowed) or i+1 (no reuse), then undo. Passing 'start' is what prevents permutations of the same set.

probs.t: Maximum Score Words Formed by Letters

patterns.name: Permutations
patterns.trigger: 'All orderings', 'arrangements', order MATTERS. n <= 10 typically (10! is about 3.6 million).
patterns.tmpl: Swap-based (swap a[i] with a[start], recurse, swap back) or used[]-array based. For duplicates, sort and skip a[i]==a[i-1] when used[i-1] is false.

probs.t: Construct the Lexicographically Largest Valid Sequence
Find the Minimum Cost Array Permutation

patterns.name: Grid / Board Backtracking
patterns.trigger: 'Does the word exist in the grid', 'collect maximum gold', 'walk over every empty cell exactly once'. Search plus undo on a 2D board.
patterns.tmpl: Mark the cell visited, recurse in four directions, then UNMARK on the way out. Prune early with a character/count check before recursing. Add a Trie when you must search many words at once.

patterns.name: Partition / Split Backtracking
patterns.trigger: 'Split the string into valid pieces', 'partition so that every part is a palindrome', 'restore IP addresses', 'all sentences from a dictionary'.
patterns.tmpl: backtrack(index): try every end position j, test isValid(s[index:j]), recurse from j. Precompute the validity table (e.g. isPalindrome DP) so the check is O(1).
patterns.cx: exponential with memo on the index

patterns.name: Pure Recursion / Divide & Conquer (no memo)
patterns.trigger: 'The k-th element in a self-similar sequence', 'the n-th row is built from the (n-1)-th', 'all results from different parenthesisations'. The structure halves or recurses on itself.
patterns.tmpl: Find the recurrence that maps position k in level n to a position in level n-1, then recurse in O(log n) or O(n) instead of building the whole structure.

probs.t: Find Kth Bit in Nth Binary String

patterns.name: Meet in the Middle
patterns.trigger: n is around 30-40 - too big for 2^n, too small for polynomial DP. 'Split into two halves with the closest sums'.
patterns.tmpl: Enumerate all 2^(n/2) subset sums of each half, sort one half, and binary search for the best complement of each element of the other. 2^40 becomes 2 * 2^20 * 20.

families.name: Dynamic Programming - Linear, Knapsack & Subsequence
families.why: DP is not memorising problems, it is naming the state. Every pattern below is defined by what its state variable means.

patterns.name: Linear DP / Take-or-Skip
patterns.trigger: A 1-D array where a choice at index i forbids or affects index i+1. 'You cannot rob two adjacent houses', 'skip the next k after using this one'.
patterns.tmpl: dp[i] = best(dp[i-1] (skip), value[i] + dp[i-2] (take)). Space-optimise to two variables once the recurrence works. Circular variants run the linear solve twice, excluding one endpoint each time.

probs.t: Maximum Total Damage With Spell Casting
Taking Maximum Energy From the Mystic Dungeon

patterns.name: Kadane & Maximum-Subarray Variants
patterns.trigger: 'Maximum sum/product of a contiguous subarray', 'best sightseeing pair', 'circular maximum subarray'.
patterns.tmpl: cur = max(a[i], cur + a[i]); best = max(best, cur). Circular: answer = max(normalKadane, totalSum - minKadane), with the all-negative edge case handled separately. For products, track both max and min.

probs.t: Maximum Absolute Sum of Any Subarray
Maximum Strength of K Disjoint Subarrays
Maximum Subarray Sum With Length Divisible by K

patterns.name: 0/1 Knapsack (subset-sum family)
patterns.trigger: Choose a subset of items, each usable AT MOST once, to hit or approach a target. 'Can the array be partitioned into two equal halves', 'assign + or - to reach target'.
patterns.tmpl: dp[i][w] = can we make w using the first i items. Iterate the weight loop BACKWARD in the 1-D space-optimised version so each item is used once. That loop direction is the whole difference from 15.4.

probs.t: Ways to Express an Integer as Sum of Powers
Maximum Value of K Coins From Piles
Partition Array Into Two Arrays to Minimize Sum Difference

patterns.name: Unbounded Knapsack / Coin Change
patterns.trigger: Items can be reused an unlimited number of times. 'Fewest coins', 'number of ways to make the amount', 'perfect squares'.
patterns.tmpl: Same table, but iterate the weight loop FORWARD. Order of the two loops decides semantics: items-outer counts combinations, target-outer counts permutations. That distinction is a classic interview trap.

probs.t: Count Ways To Build Good Strings
Minimum Sum of Values by Dividing Array

patterns.name: Longest Increasing Subsequence & Variants
patterns.trigger: 'Longest subsequence that is increasing / chainable / divisible / within a difference'. Subsequence, not subarray.
patterns.tmpl: O(n^2): dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over j<i with a valid relation. O(n log n): maintain 'tails' and binary search the replacement position. When the relation is a value gap, a hashmap dp keyed by value is often O(n).

Minimum Number of Removals to Make Mountain Array
Find the Longest Valid Obstacle Course at Each Position

patterns.name: Subsequence DP with a Pair State
patterns.trigger: The transition needs the LAST TWO chosen elements: Fibonacci-like subsequences, arithmetic subsequences, alternating parity.
patterns.tmpl: dp[j][i] = length of the best subsequence ending with the pair (j, i). Hash values to indices so you can look up the required predecessor in O(1).

patterns.trigger: 'You may hold at most one share', 'cooldown of one day', 'at most k transactions', or any problem with a small set of modes and legal transitions.
patterns.tmpl: Name the states (holding / free / cooling), write one recurrence per state, iterate. Drawing the 3-node transition diagram before coding removes almost all the bugs.

families.name: Dynamic Programming - Grids, Strings, Intervals & Counting
families.why: Two-dimensional DP. The state is almost always 'a prefix of A and a prefix of B' or 'the subrange [i..j]'.

patterns.name: DP on Grids (paths)
patterns.trigger: Move only right/down (or a fixed direction set) through a matrix, optimising or counting paths.
patterns.tmpl: dp[i][j] = f(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Roll to a single row for O(m) space. When two agents move simultaneously, the state becomes (row, col1, col2) because both are on the same row at every step.

probs.t: Maximum Non Negative Product in a Matrix
Paths in Matrix Whose Sum Is Divisible by K
Maximum Amount of Money Robot Can Earn
Find the Maximum Number of Fruits Collected

patterns.name: LCS Family (two sequences)
patterns.trigger: Two strings/arrays plus 'common', 'edit', 'delete to make equal', 'interleaving', 'shortest string containing both'.
patterns.tmpl: dp[i][j] over the two prefixes. Characters match -> 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise take the best of skipping one side. Reconstruct the actual string by walking the table backwards.

probs.t: Minimum ASCII Delete Sum for Two Strings
Max Dot Product of Two Subsequences

patterns.name: Palindromic DP
patterns.trigger: 'Longest palindromic substring/subsequence', 'minimum insertions to make it a palindrome', 'count palindromic substrings'.
patterns.tmpl: dp[i][j] = is s[i..j] a palindrome, filled by increasing length. Longest palindromic SUBSEQUENCE = LCS(s, reverse(s)). Expand-around-centre is the O(n^2)/O(1)-space alternative for substrings.

probs.t: Minimum Insertion Steps to Make a String Palindrome

patterns.name: Interval DP / Matrix Chain (split at k)
patterns.trigger: 'Merge/burst/cut the range and the cost depends on the whole remaining segment'. You must decide which element is handled LAST, not first.
patterns.tmpl: dp[i][j] = min/max over k in (i,j) of dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + cost(i,k,j). Iterate by increasing length. Adding sentinel values at both ends usually removes the boundary cases.

probs.t: Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick
Number of Ways of Cutting a Pizza

patterns.name: Partition DP (split an array into groups)
patterns.trigger: 'Divide the array into k subarrays', 'partition into groups of at most k and each becomes its maximum', 'break the string into dictionary words'.
patterns.tmpl: dp[i] = best over j of dp[j] + cost(j+1..i). Bound the inner loop by the problem's group-size limit. When the cost is monotone, a deque or heap collapses the inner loop (see 17.3).

probs.t: Minimum Difficulty of a Job Schedule
Check if There is a Valid Partition For The Array
Minimum Sum of Values by Dividing Array

patterns.name: Counting DP (number of ways, mod 1e9+7)
patterns.trigger: 'How many ways', 'count the arrangements', answer 'modulo 10^9 + 7'. The mod is a giveaway that you are counting, not optimising.
patterns.tmpl: Same recurrences as optimisation DP but with '+' instead of 'min/max'. Take the mod after every addition. Watch the base case: dp[0] = 1 (one way to do nothing).

probs.t: Number of Dice Rolls With Target Sum
Number of Ways to Stay in the Same Place After Some Steps
Count Ways To Build Good Strings
Painting a Grid With Three Different Colors

patterns.name: Game Theory DP (minimax on ranges)
patterns.trigger: 'Two players take turns', 'both play optimally', 'the winner is whoever has the larger score'. Almost always an interval or index-based DP.
patterns.tmpl: dp[i][j] = the best score DIFFERENCE the player to move can achieve on [i..j]. The opponent's optimal play appears as a minus sign: dp[i][j] = max(a[i] - dp[i+1][j], a[j] - dp[i][j-1]).

patterns.name: Probability / Expectation DP
patterns.trigger: 'Probability that ...', 'expected value', 'the knight stays on the board'. Answers are floats, not counts.
patterns.tmpl: dp[state] = sum over transitions of P(transition) * dp[next]. Watch for absorbing states and for precision-based early termination when probabilities decay fast.

families.name: Dynamic Programming - Advanced
families.why: These four patterns separate the top 5% in contests. Each is recognisable from the constraints alone.

patterns.name: Bitmask DP
patterns.trigger: THE tell: n <= 20 (sometimes 22) combined with 'assign every item', 'visit every node', 'cover all requirements'. 2^20 is about 1e6, which is exactly why the limit is 20.
patterns.tmpl: dp[mask][extra] where mask is the set of used/visited items. Iterate masks in increasing order; transitions add one unset bit. Enumerate submasks with sub=(sub-1)&mask when you need set partitions.
patterns.cx: O(2^n * n) or O(3^n) for submask DP

patterns.name: Digit DP
patterns.trigger: 'Count numbers in [L, R] with property P'. The range is up to 1e9-1e18, so you cannot iterate. You iterate over DIGITS instead.
patterns.tmpl: dfs(pos, tight, started, extraState) over the digit string, memoised on (pos, extraState) for the non-tight case. Answer f(R) - f(L-1). Handle leading zeros with a 'started' flag.

patterns.trigger: A correct O(n^2) DP whose transition is 'best dp[j] over a contiguous or monotone range of j'. n is 1e5, so the inner loop must go.
patterns.tmpl: Sliding window max -> monotonic deque. Best over any prefix by a secondary key -> BIT/segment tree. Best-k so far -> heap with lazy deletion. Write the O(n^2) first, then swap in the structure.

families.name: Greedy
families.why: Greedy is the hardest family to trust. The discipline: state the exchange argument out loud before you code, or fall back to DP.

patterns.name: Exchange-Argument Greedy (sort by a clever key)
patterns.trigger: Order-dependent objective. 'Arrange the numbers to form the largest number', 'plant in the best order', 'process the jobs so total time is minimised'.
patterns.tmpl: Find the pairwise comparator that a local swap would improve, then sort by it. Concatenation order, deadline/growth-time descending, and ratio sorting are the three you will see most.

patterns.name: Local-Decision Greedy with an Invariant
patterns.trigger: 'Can you reach the end', 'minimum jumps', 'is there a valid starting station'. One forward pass while tracking a reachability or deficit invariant.
patterns.tmpl: Track the farthest reachable index (or the running deficit). For minimum jumps, treat it as a BFS over levels: when i hits the current level end, increment the answer and set the new end to farthest.

patterns.name: Greedy + Heap (revocable decisions)
patterns.trigger: Take greedily, but you may UNDO an earlier choice when a better one appears. 'Use ladders on the k largest gaps', 'replace the worst pick'.
patterns.tmpl: Push every choice into a heap as you make it; when you exceed the budget, pop the worst and convert it. This 'regret' pattern turns an intractable global optimisation into O(n log n).

patterns.name: Lexicographic / Constructive Greedy
patterns.trigger: 'Build the lexicographically smallest/largest valid result', 'partition so each letter appears in only one part', 'reorganise so no two adjacent are equal'.
patterns.tmpl: Decide position by position, always taking the best character that still leaves a feasible completion. Feasibility is usually checked with remaining counts or a last-occurrence table. Heaps handle the 'no two adjacent' variants.

patterns.trigger: The answer depends only on the frequency histogram, not on the order: task scheduling with cooldown, minimum rounds, pairing up characters into palindromes.
patterns.tmpl: Count first, then apply a closed-form or a small greedy over the counts. Task Scheduler's ceil-based formula and the odd/even palindrome split are the two archetypes.

families.name: Bit Manipulation
families.why: Bits show up in three disguises: as a cheap set, as independent columns, and as a greedy construction from the high bit down. Contests love all three.

patterns.name: Core Bit Tricks & XOR Pairing
patterns.trigger: 'Every element appears twice except one', 'count set bits', 'is it a power of two', 'complement'. Small, self-contained bit identities.
patterns.tmpl: Memorise: x & (x-1) clears the lowest set bit; x & -x isolates it; a^a=0 and a^0=a; x & (x-1) == 0 tests a power of two. For 'appears three times except one', count bits per position mod 3.

patterns.name: Bit-by-Bit Greedy Construction
patterns.trigger: 'Build the minimum/maximum number satisfying a bit condition', 'the smallest x with the same number of set bits', 'minimise the XOR'.
patterns.tmpl: Decide bits from the most significant down. At each bit, take the value that helps the objective if it does not break feasibility. Count remaining set bits carefully when the popcount is constrained.

patterns.trigger: 'Maximum XOR of any two numbers', 'the best XOR partner for each query', values up to 2^30.
patterns.tmpl: Insert each number into a binary trie MSB-first. To maximise, greedily walk toward the opposite bit at every level. Add counts per node to support deletions and range restrictions.

patterns.trigger: 'gcd', 'coprime', 'prime factors', 'divisible by', or a value bound around 1e5-1e6 that begs for a sieve.
patterns.tmpl: Sieve of Eratosthenes with the smallest-prime-factor array gives O(log n) factorisation per query. gcd(a,b) with Euclid. Modular inverse by Fermat: pow(a, MOD-2, MOD) when MOD is prime.

families.why: Strings are where sliding window, DP, tries and hashing all meet. This family collects the string-specific machinery that does not fit elsewhere.

patterns.trigger: 'Find all occurrences of a pattern', 'is the string a repetition of a substring', 'the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix', 'minimum characters to prepend to make it a palindrome'.
patterns.tmpl: LPS array: lps[i] = the longest proper prefix of s[0..i] that is also a suffix. Build in O(n), then match without ever moving the text pointer backwards. n % (n - lps[n-1]) == 0 tests periodicity.

patterns.trigger: Compare many substrings for equality, 'do all 2^k binary codes appear', 'find both a pattern and another pattern within distance k'.
patterns.tmpl: h(s) = sum s[i] * base^i mod a large prime. Slide by removing the leading term and adding the new one. Use two independent mods when collisions would be fatal.
